### Exercise

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2032.png)

```jsx
const _ = {};
_.each = function (list, callback) {
  if (Array.isArray(list)) {
    // loop through array
    for (let index = 0; index < array.length; index++) {

      // call the callback with a list item
      callback(list[i], i, list);
    }
  } else {
    // loop through object
  }
};

_.each(["sally", "georgia", "porgie"], function (name, i, list) {
  if (list([i + 1])) {
    console.log(name, "is younger than", list[i + 1]);
  } else {
    console.log(name, "is the oldest");
  }
});
```

1. Until now we have dealt with array part.
    1. Where we have conditioned to check for array and then if it is we are passing aruguments to **callback** i.e. list with each index, current index and whole list.
    2. Reason for passing all of this might be to make sure we have all the things available in the function. 
2. We are checking if we have made the code correctly or not.

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2033.png)

1. Adding object option as well

```jsx
const _ = {};
_.each = function (list, callback) {
  if (Array.isArray(list)) {
    // loop through array
    for (let index = 0; index < array.length; index++) {
      const element = array[index];
      // call the callback with a list item
      callback(list[i], i, list);
    }
  } else {
    // loop through object
    for (var key in list) {
      callback(list[key], key, list);
    }
  }
};

_.each(["sally", "georgia", "porgie"], function (name, i, list) {
  if (list([i + 1])) {
    console.log(name, "is younger than", list[i + 1]);
  } else {
    console.log(name, "is the oldest");
  }
});
```

    1. Implementing the .map function
    
    ```jsx
    _.map = function(list, callback){
    	//create an empty array to store
    	var storage = [];
    	// looping 
    	for(var i = 0; i < list.length ; i++){
    		// callback(element)
    		// push it into our array
    		storage.push(callback(list[i], i, list))
    	} 
    	//return []
    	return storage;	
    
    }
    ```
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2040.png)
    
    1. Similar implementation using each loop
        
        ```jsx
        _.map = function(list, callback){
        	//create an empty array to store
        	var storage = [];
        	// looping 
        	_.each(list,function(v, i, list){
        		storage.push(callback(v, i, list));
        	}) 
        	//return []
        	return storage;	
        
        }
        ```
        

### filter

1. It takes an array and a callback and returns a new array which contains only parts of array that return true from the callback of the filter function.
2. The callback has to return boolean either true or false depedning on the callback condition. If it returns true we are gonna save the array otherwise not.
3. It size can be lesser or equal ( in rare cases )  to the original array.

### Implementing our own filter function

```jsx
const _ = {};
_.filter = function(arr, cb){
	// create a new array 
	const storage = [];
	// loop through the array 
		for (let i = 0; i < arr.lenght ; i++){
		// check if the cb returns true 
			if(cb(arr[i], i, arr) === true){
				// if returns true push into array
				storage.push(arr[i])
			}
		}
	// returns array3
	return storage;
}
```

### Implementing our own filter function Using _.each

```jsx
const _ = {};
_.filter = function(arr, cb){
	// create a new array 
	const storage = [];
	// loop through the array 
	_.each(arr,function(val, i, list){
		if(cb(val, i, list)){
				// if returns true push into array
				storage.push(val)
			}
	})
	// returns array3
	return storage;
}
```

### ES6 Arrow Functions

1. Binds the context ( the value that “**this”** has to its parent context )
2. It does not own its own keyword ( this ) unlike normal functions which have their own keyword (this) that gets bound at call time.
    1. So Arrow fucntions do not have their own value for **(this) which they inherit, they reach upto their parent scope** and grab value for this ( keyword ) 
3. It also have no value for arguments keyword. The argument keyword gets bound to all arguments being passed to a fucntion at calltime.

**Best Practice:** always use return statement in the arrow function.

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2074.png)

1. Execution context contains two more things Memory → Variable Environment ( variables and functions are stored as key value pairs ) and Code → Thread of Execution ( Code is executed here one line at a time ).
2. Another core Js concept as → Single-threaded means only single line of code can be executed at a time. While synchronous means in a specific order. Which means next line will only be executed once current line has been executed.

### How JS is Executed and Call Stack

- Code Example
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2076.png)
    
    1. First of all a **Global Execution Context** is created.
    2. Which consists of Variable Environment ( Memory ) and Thread of Execution ( Code ).
    3. The Execution Context is created in two phases.
        
        ### Memory Creation Phase
        
        > Memory is allocated to all variables and functions
        > 
        1. In our case stores n → variable as key and its value as undefined.
        2. While function square name as key and whole code ( square function ) as its value.
        3. Here the way all functions are stored is different. Sqaure2 and Sqaure4 are stored as undefined as contrary to square function whose whole value is stored.
            
            ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2077.png)
            
        4. The difference is because of the fact that square2 and square4 are variables while square is a function only.
        
        
        ### Code Execution Phase
        
        > Again Js runs through whole code line-by-line.
        > 
        1. Variable n value of undefined is replaced by actual value of 2.
        2. Function square is same as it was before.
        3. at line 6 square2’s value is square function being invoked
        - This results in creation of another brand new execution context ( specific to that function )
            1.  Again in there are similar two phases first is memory creation of assigning undefined to variables.
                
                ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2078.png)
                
            
            b. Then code execution phase where we will each execute each line.
            
            c. First value of n i.e. 2 is passed to num **( where n is argument to square and num is parameter )**
            
            d. Then this line of ans i.e num * num is executed to give back result to ans variable. 
            
            ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2079.png)
            
            ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2080.png)
            
        1. When we see return statement in square it means to return control of program where function was invoked in GEC ( Global Execution Context ).
        2. So return statement takes value of ans → 4 and assigns it to Square2 in Code Execution Phase of GEC.
            
            ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2081.png)
            
        - Again new Function Execution Context will be created for sqaure4 as square(4) fucntion was invoked.
            1. Similar steps will be followed for Memory Creation Phase and Code Execution phase following it.
                
                ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2082.png)
                
                ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2083.png)
                
                Finally a return 
                
                ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2084.png)
                
        1. Finally square4 is assigned return value of ans and GEC is deleted finally.
        
        1. How does JS Manages to go through all these steps like Creation, Deletion and Passing Control etc. 
    - All this happens because of Call Stack
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%2085.png)
        
        1. The GEC is at bottom of Call Stack as its the last one to be executed as in our case.

        1. again Square for sqaure4

## Lexical Environment
 
![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20117.png)

1. Global EC is pushed into Call Stack.
2. Function ***a*** assigned its whole code into memory creation phase. While in code execution phase a  new EC → function ***a*** is pushed into Call Stack.

1. where b is assigned undefined in MC phase and then value 10 in Code Execution phase. Where as same for function c and then its EC is pushed to stack.

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20120.png)

> Wen an EC is created a lexical environment is created. It is nothing but local memory along with Lexical Environment of its parent.
> 

Like ***function c*** is lexically inside **function a** and function is lexically present in Global Execution Context.

1. **Function c** has access to lexical environment of **function a** which means local memory of a and lexical environment of Global Execution Context. 
2. The orange box represents local memory + lexical environment of parent.

### Let and Const + Temporal Dead Zone

### Let and Constant Declarations are hoisted

> Its true but its entirely different then the var hoisting. Actually they are in the temporal dead zone for the time being.
> 
- Example
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20123.png)
    
    1. Revising some basics as var variables are hoisted as undefined even before code is executed.
    2. When we try to access a before its defined we get initialization error ( strange ).
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20124.png)
    
    1. So how to find if it was even hoisted or not.
    2. If we use browser to look into memory, we can see a and b are assigned undefined in Memory Creation phase though they are in different spaces ( b in GEC and a in Script )
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20125.png)
        
    1. variables declared with let and const are ==not stored GEC but some other memory space. They have some separate memory space where they have reserved memory space thus we cannot access the until they are initialized some value.==
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20126.png)
        
    2. Now a is assigned a value of 10.

### Temporal Dead Zone

> The time since when it was hoisted to time until it was initialized with a value.
> 

### Reference Error

> Accessing a variable within its temporal dead zone gives rise to a reference error.
> 

> It will also rise when we access a variable not even defined in our code.
> 

Although error message will be different in both cases.

1. Trying to access a variable ( defined using let and const ) though global object window or this returns undefined.
2. Because its defined in other memory space than GEC.

### Syntax Error

> We cannot re declare a variable defined using let.
> 
> 
> ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20127.png)
> 

It does not matter if this declaration is done either using var or let 

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20128.png)

There is no such error in case var declaration and re declaration. 

> In case of syntax error JS code do not even runs a single line at all.
> 

In case of Const we have to declare and define variable at same line unlike let which can be declared and then defined later on.

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20129.png)

This syntax error demands that initalizer is missing on line 4 where b is declared only.

### Type Error

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20130.png)

If we try to re assign a value to a constant variable we get Type Error.

| Reference Error | Syntax Error | Type Error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trying to find / access a variable in a memory space we cannot access. | Violating standard way of performing some action or defining something  | When violating the rule of a specific type. |

| Const | Let  | Var |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recommended to be used always or whenever possible. Specially in cases where we do not want to re assign values to a variable. | Second preference is let wherever possible because of its TDZ, will not run into un expected errors. | least recommended to be used because of how much error prone it can be sometimes. |
- How to avoid Temporal Dead Zones
    
    > Always have declarations at top of the code.
    >

### Shadowing in JS

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20136.png)

1. If we try to print a inside block it will be 10 as it shadows the same variable a outside block. Why ? Because JS looks for a first in local memory and then lexical environment of parent. 
2. Also if we print a after block value is 10 again, Why ? because value of var is global so is modified by var a of the block thus its 10 now.
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20137.png)
    
3. All these rules are not applicable for let though.
4. We can see using let we have outer let having Scrip scope while inner let as Block Scope.
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20138.png)
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20139.png)
    
5. We expect similar behavior in case of constant. 

> Shadowing is not only limited to Block Scope, works similar with Functional Scopes as well.
> 

### Illegal Shadowing

![An example of illegal shadowing](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20140.png)

An example of illegal shadowing

1. Using let to declare a outside block and then using same name to declare using var outside is not gonna work, Why ? 
2. Because var has global scope as in Global scope it contradicts with let a.
3. So we can do it using let inside block as well. 

![Legal Shadowing](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20141.png)

Legal Shadowing

1. If var on global and let on local → Legal shadowing.

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20142.png)

### Details

The whole problem of Illegal Shadowing arises from the fact that the varaible shadowing should not cross its scope boundary. Like in case of outer let and inner var → var has still GEC while if same var was in function it would have FEC and thus would be legal shadowing.

### setTimeout + Closures

1. This function prints 1 after three seconds ( 1000ms = 1s )
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20150.png)
    
2. Here Namaste JS will be printed first then it wait 1s to log value of i.e. 1.
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20151.png)
    

> JS waits for nothing and just moves on.
> 
- What happens BTS ?
    1. setTimeout actually stores this callback function ( which is along with its local environment + lexical scope of parent ) somewhere in the memory attached with timer.
    2. Then JS moves on to execute other things.
    3. Once the timer expires setTimeout picks the function again and puts it in the call stack to run it.
    
- Example ( Print numbers→ respective after each second )
    1. This code where we start with 1 till 5 while at each step multiple with i to make sure each element gets printed at its seconds passed. But does it works this way ?
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20152.png)
    
    1. It prints 6, five times, each 6 after ith second. 
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20153.png)
    
    1. What happens is in first iteration and so on, the setTimeout stores this function with its closure to some place binding timer. All these five copies of same function point to same value of ***i***.
    2. Thus after last iteration reference of ***i*** updates to 6, that is why until 1 second passes loops are already run ( **as JS waits for none** ) and value of ***i*** is set to 6. so it prints values 6, five times.
    
    ### Solution with let
    
    > Use let instead of var.
    > 
    1. ***Let*** has a block scope and in every iteration a new value of ***i*** is assigned to each respective function copy thus now it prints correct values.
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20154.png)
    
    ### Solution with var
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20155.png)
    
    1. Enclose the setTimeout in other function, now supply i as an argument to this function, which in return produces a new copy and thus setTimeout callack has reference to new value of i and not similar value.

### Callback function

> Since functions are first class citizens thus when they are passed to another fucntion they are called as **Callback function.**
> 

### Advantages

1. Give access to Asynchronous World while being in a synchronous single threaded language. 
2. The reason we call some function as callback is because of the fact that since they are now part of  some other function so they can be called later on anywhere in the code.

### Best Practice

1. Use asynchronous operations where ever the code is taking a longer time to execute.
2. Thus it is bad practice to stop or halt or block the Main Thread of Execution in Js.

### **Asynchronous JavaScript & EVENT LOOP**

1. When does the event loop actually start? - Event loop, as the name suggests, is a single-thread, loop that is `almost infinite`. It's always running and doing its job.
2.  Are only asynchronous web API callbacks are registered in the web API environment? - YES, the synchronous callback functions like what we pass inside map, filter, and reduce aren't registered in the Web API environment. It's just those async callback functions that go through all this.
3. Does the web API environment stores only the callback function and pushes the same callback to queue/microtask queue? - Yes, the callback functions are stored, and a reference is scheduled in the queues. Moreover, in the case of event listeners(for example click handlers), the original callbacks stay in the web API environment forever, that's why it's advised to explicitly remove the listeners when not in use so that the garbage collector does its job.
4. How does it matter if we delay for setTimeout would be 0ms. Then callback will move to queue without any wait? 
No, there are trust issues with setTimeout()

. The callback function needs to wait until the Call Stack is empty. So the 0 ms callback might have to wait for 100ms also if the stack is busy.  It's a very beautiful concept, and I've covered this in detail in the next episode of Namaste JavaScript.

### Creating a Promise, Promise Chaining and Error Handling

```jsx
const cart = ["shoes", "pants", "kurta"];

const promise = createOrder(cart);
console.log(promise);
promise
  .then(function (orderId) {
    console.log(orderId);
    return orderId;
  })
  .then(function (orderId) {
    return proceedToPayment(orderId);
  })
  .then(function (paymentInfo) {
    console.log(paymentInfo);
  })
  .catch(function (err) {
    console.log(err.message);
  });

// Producer

function createOrder(cart) {
  const pr = new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
    // create an order
    // validate card
    // orderId
    if (!validateCard(cart)) {
      const err = new Error("Cart is not valid");
      reject(err);
    }
    // logic for createOrder
    const orderId = "12345";
    if (orderId) {
      setTimeout(function () {
        resolve(orderId);
      }, 5000);
    }
  });
  return pr;
}

function validateCard(cart) {
  return true;
}

function proceedToPayment(orderId) {
  return new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
    resolve("Payment Successful");
  });
}
```

### Further Explanation by Chat GPT

The reason why the expression **`[100, 2, 45].sort()`** does not sort the array in the expected way is because the **`sort()`** method sorts an array in lexicographic order by default, which means that it sorts the array elements as strings based on their Unicode code points.

To sort an array of numbers in ascending order, you can pass a sorting function as an argument to the **`sort()`** method that compares the numeric values of the array elements. Here's an example:

```
cssCopy code
[100, 2, 45].sort((a, b) => a - b); // returns [2, 45, 100]

```

In this example, the sorting function subtracts **`b`** from **`a`**, which will result in a negative value if **`a`** is less than **`b`**, a positive value if **`a`** is greater than **`b`**, and zero if **`a`** is equal to **`b`**. This will cause the **`sort()`** method to sort the array in ascending order based on the numeric values of the elements.

[](data:image/svg+xml,%3csvg%20xmlns=%27http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%27%20version=%271.1%27%20width=%2730%27%20height=%2730%27/%3e)

can you explain lexicographic and Unicode further in simple terms

Sure, I'd be happy to explain lexicographic order and Unicode in simple terms!

Lexicographic order is a way of comparing and ordering strings based on the alphabetical order of their characters. In lexicographic order, the first character of each string is compared, and if they are different, the string with the "lower" (earlier in the alphabet) character comes first. If the first characters are the same, the second characters are compared, and so on, until either all characters have been compared or a difference is found.

For example, in lexicographic order, "apple" comes before "banana" because "a" comes before "b" in the alphabet. However, "apple" comes after "app" because "e" comes after "p" in the alphabet.

Unicode is a system for encoding characters in a computer. Each character is assigned a unique number, called a code point, which can be represented in binary form. The code points are organized into blocks, such as the Latin block for characters used in Western languages, the Cyrillic block for characters used in Slavic languages, and so on.

In JavaScript, the **`sort()`** method sorts strings and arrays of strings in lexicographic order by default. When sorting an array of numbers, the **`sort()`** method converts the numbers to strings and sorts them in lexicographic order. This can lead to unexpected results if the array contains numbers that are not the same length, such as **`[100, 2, 45]`**, because lexicographic order compares the strings character by character, rather than comparing the numeric values of the numbers.

// TODO 4: Declare disable & enable functions to set or remove the "disabled" attribute from a given button element
    // disable(button) should set the button element's attribute "disabled" to the value ""
    // enable(button) should remove the attribute "disabled" from the button element
    function disable(optionButtons) {
      for (let i = 0; i < optionButtons.length; i++) {
        optionButtons[i].setAttribute("disabled", "");
      }
    }

    function enable(optionButtons) {
      for (let i = 0; i < optionButtons.length; i++) {
        optionButtons[i].removeAttribute("disabled");
      }
    }

      } else {

### Map and Filter

- The speaker introduces the concepts of map, filter, and reduce as useful methods for iterating over arrays.
- Map applies a function to each item in an array and returns a new array with the results, without mutating the original array.
- Filter removes items from an array based on some condition, returning a new array without the removed items.
- Reduce combines all items in an array into a single value.
- Arrow functions are commonly used when passing functions as arguments to map and filter.
- Template literals, which use backticks instead of quotes, allow for interpolation of variables and expressions in strings.

### Spread

- The spread syntax in JavaScript uses three dots to expand the contents of an iterable object, such as an array or a string.
- It can be used to expand an array into another array, which is similar to the concat method.
- When passing arguments into a function, the spread syntax can be used to pass in multiple values separated by commas.
- Push method modifies the original array, while the concat method creates a new one.
- The spread syntax can be used to log out items on one line, rather than as an array object.
- It can be a useful alternative to looping over an array to pull out each element individually.

### Loops ( Continued )

[JavaScript First Steps](https://anjana.dev/javascript-first-steps/3-slides.html#/3/1)

- A while loop is a control flow statement that allows code to be executed repeatedly based on a given condition
- The basic syntax of a while loop is **`while (condition) { ... }`**, where the code inside the braces will be executed repeatedly as long as the condition is true
- It's important to make sure the condition of the while loop will eventually be false, or else the loop will execute indefinitely, resulting in an infinite loop
- You can use break statements within a while loop to exit the loop early if a certain condition is met
- You can also use continue statements within a while loop to skip over certain iterations of the loop based on a certain condition
- The do-while loop is a similar construct to the while loop, but it ensures that the code inside the loop will be executed at least once, regardless of whether the initial condition is true or false
- While loops and do-while loops are useful for iterating through arrays, processing data, and performing other tasks that require repeated execution of code until a certain condition is met.

        function getRandomElement(array) {
            const i = Math.floor(Math.random() * array.length);
            return array[i];
        }

        // Utility function to shuffle the order of items in an array in-place
        function shuffleArray(array) {
            return array.sort((a, b) => Math.random() - 0.5);
        }

// TODO 1
        // Given an array of possible answers, a correct answer value, and a number of choices to get,
        // return a list of that many choices, including the correct answer and others from the array
        function getMultipleChoices(n, correctAnswer, possibleChoices) {
            // Use a while loop and the getRandomElement() function
            // Make sure there are no duplicates in the possibleChoices
            const choices = [];
            choices.push(correctAnswer);
            while (choices.length < n) {
                let candidate = getRandomElement(possibleChoices);
                if (!choices.includes(candidate)) {
                    choices.push(candidate);
                }
            }
            return shuffleArray(choices);

        }

### Asynchronous Code

1. In real world we would not want to wait for something in JS to finish up before we can interact with it.
2. In this transcript, the speaker talks about asynchronous and synchronous code in JavaScript. They explain how time works in JavaScript and how certain code can take longer to execute than others, which can make JavaScript freeze. However, JavaScript is single-threaded, so it can only execute one task at a time. To avoid freezing the web browser, JavaScript adds long tasks to a to-do list and continues executing other code while waiting to execute the long task later.

[JavaScript First Steps](https://anjana.dev/javascript-first-steps/3-slides.html#/4)

[Introducing asynchronous JavaScript - Learn web development | MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/JavaScript/Asynchronous/Introducing)

### APIs and Fetch

[JavaScript First Steps](https://anjana.dev/javascript-first-steps/3-slides.html#/5)

- Fetching data in JavaScript can take a lot of time, but we can tell JavaScript to make the browser fetch the data we need.
- URLs point to resources on the web, such as web pages, images, or data.
- APIs, or application programming interfaces, are services that expose data at certain URLs. We often find data we need for our programs from APIs.
- APIs have a structure that the API developer will document, including endpoints, which are specific URLs that give us particular resources.
- We can access API endpoints in our browser to see what data the API returns. APIs often return data in JSON format.
- Once we have data from an API endpoint in our program, we can work with it like any other data, such as filtering or mapping an array.

### Promises

[JavaScript First Steps](https://anjana.dev/javascript-first-steps/3-slides.html#/6)

- The fetch function is used to retrieve a resource or data from a URL in JavaScript.
- Fetch returns a promise, which represents a value that is not available yet.
- Promises can be in three states: pending, fulfilled, or rejected.
- A pending state means that the promise is waiting for the value to be retrieved.
- A fulfilled state means that the promise has succeeded and the value is available.
- A rejected state means that the promise has failed to retrieve the value.
- Promises are used for asynchronous code, which involves operations that take time to complete.
- Fetch is an example of a function that returns a promise, but promises can also be used in other contexts.

### Await

[JavaScript First Steps](https://anjana.dev/javascript-first-steps/3-slides.html#/7)

- await tells JavaScript to wait for an asynchronous operation to finish before continuing to run the code.
- When we call **`fetch()`**, we get back a promise.
- If we use **`await`** before the **`fetch()`** call, we're telling JavaScript to wait for the promise to be resolved before continuing to run the code.
- The value that **`fetch()`** returns is a promise, but what we really want is the value that the promise resolves to, which is a response object.
- The response object has a **`body`** property, which contains the response body as a readable stream.
- To read the data from the response body, we can use the **`json()`** method on the response object, which returns another promise that resolves to a JavaScript object.
- The **`json()`** method reads the stream of bytes from the response body and parses it as a JSON object that JavaScript can work with.
- Like the **`fetch()`** method, the **`json()`** method also returns a promise, so we need to use **`await`** to wait for the promise to resolve before continuing to run the code.
- Once we have the JSON object, we can manipulate it in our code as needed.

### De-structuring

[JavaScript First Steps](https://anjana.dev/javascript-first-steps/3-slides.html#/8)

- The transcript is about de-structuring in JavaScript, which is a syntax used to break down an object into its individual properties.
- It is a way of declaring multiple variables at once or extracting properties from an object and making them variables in the current scope.
- De-structuring can be handy when there are many properties in an object, and only some of them are required.
- It is a shorthand for getting the object and using dots to access its properties.
- In JavaScript, object properties are not ordered, unlike items in an array, which are ordered.
- The order of variables inside the curly braces doesn't matter when de-structuring.
- It also works for arrays but in specific order unlike objects.
- Also we can use spread operator to paste or unfold values of an array or object inside an array.
-

### Thread of Execution and Memory

JavaScript has two parts to cater a given code 

***Thread of Execution*** → Going through the code line-by-line and doing it.

***Memory*** → having a place to save stuff that shows up like data, variables, functions etc. 

They are called as ***Execution Context.***

> Every function has a brand new execution context besides Global EC.
>

### Call Stack

In JavaScript, a call stack is a mechanism used to keep track of function calls and their corresponding contexts. Whenever a function is called, a new frame is added to the top of the call stack, and when the function returns, the frame is removed from the top of the stack.

Here's a simple code example that demonstrates how the call stack works:

```jsx

function add(x, y) {
  return x + y;
}

function multiply(x, y) {
  return x * y;
}

function square(x) {
  return multiply(x, x);
}

function calculate(a, b, c) {
  const result = add(a, b);
  const squaredResult = square(result);
  return multiply(squaredResult, c);
}

const finalResult = calculate(2, 3, 4);
console.log(finalResult); // Output: 100

```

In this example, we have four functions: **`add`**, **`multiply`**, **`square`**, and **`calculate`**. The **`calculate`** function calls the other three functions to perform some mathematical operations.

When the **`calculate`** function is called, it gets added to the call stack. Inside the function, the **`add`** function is called, which also gets added to the call stack. When the **`add`** function returns, it is removed from the top of the stack, and the **`square`** function is called, which gets added to the stack. When the **`square`** function returns, it is removed from the top of the stack, and the **`multiply`** function is called, which also gets added to the stack. Finally, when the **`multiply`** function returns, it is removed from the top of the stack, and the **`calculate`** function returns the final result.

> Keep track of the functions we’re running and where our thread of execution is using Call Stack.
>

> Functions are used to make a piece of code re-usable so as to follow the dry principle.

- What is Parameter
    
    > Because parameter allows functions to apply same logic to different data anytime.

    It is like writing code one time containing a blank logic only to evaluate once that piece of actually runs. 
    
    *So parameters actually allows us to write code without deciding what data to be needed until that code actually runs.*
    

What if we could leave little bit of our code, unevaluated until the code actually runs. Similar to parameters but only this time its not ***To Be Decided*** data but some code. 

- This is where ***Higher Order Functions***.
- Repeating Functionality
    - Line by Line Thread of Execution and Memory view of code

    function copyArrayAndMultiplyBy2(array) {
    	const output = [];
    	for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) 
    	{
    		output.push(array[i] * 2);
    	}
    return output;
    }
    const myArray = [1,2,3];
    const result = copyArrayAndMultiplyBy2(myArray);
    ```

### **Enforcing Dry ( Solution to invalidating DRY )**

- So to enforce **DRY** ( Do not Repeat Yourself ) we have to pass that specific functionality to our function because its the only one changing every time. But in JS we cannot plain String directly thus we need to wrap our functionality in something i.e. A function so that we can pass it to our function and call it with argument as array values. That function wrapper will contain our specific logics like multiply, divide etc.
- Higher Order Functions
    - As in previous example if we want to add a number *n* to each value of array or dividing each value by *n.*
    - In all these cases although we are using a function but still repeating whole function every time only for a small line.
    - We can pass array as one argument and a logic wrapping our functionality like adding or multiplying or dividing etc. as another argument.
    
    ```jsx
    function copyArrayAndManipulate(array, instructions) {
        const output = [];
        for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) {
        output.push(instructions(array[i]));
        }
        return output;
        }
        function multiplyBy2(input) { return input * 2; }
        const result = copyArrayAndManipulate([1, 2, 3], multiplyBy2);
    ```
    
    > So it is what Higher Order Function is simply.
    > 
    - This function is passed as a reference or a link back to that function.

How can we pass functions as arguments to other functions

![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20263.png)

Functions are passed as a reference so that the instruction refer to multiplyBy2 function and does not copy it. 

> Functions are first class objects. This means they can be treated just like objects
> 

> mutliplyBy2 is a callback while copyArrayAndManipulate is Higher Order Function
>

### Closure

[I never understood JavaScript closures](https://medium.com/dailyjs/i-never-understood-javascript-closures-9663703368e8)

1. Functions when run create an execution context temporarily and gets removed after its execution except returned value. So they do not remember their last executions or anything from previous executions. But what if it could remember it? what if functions have memory
2. This allows the function to have persistent/cache memory.
- Intuition
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20264.png)
    
    - Here when createFunction returns multiplyBy2 its just a label so it does not know what it is until it moves back to local memory and sees that multiplyBy2 is a function so it return function definition or code or value and not the identifier i.e. multiplyBy2 to the generatedFunc identifier in global memory.
    - generatedFunc has no connection to createFunc and was yes created by it and then moves on. Actually running generatedFunc is to run function that was born as multiplyBy2. Simply it has no connection to createdFunc but is connected only with multiplyBy.
    - The EC of createFunc was deleted and multiplyBy2 label as well with it. Now if we want to access it we need to use it through generatedFunc
    - since js is synchronous when it has processed createFunc it never going back to that function again, but how it gets argument → num set to parameter → 3 then which is inside createFunc definition back in previous lines of code ? as we said we said js cannot go back.
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20265.png)
        
    - Js saved the definition of multiplyBy2 in generatedFunc, everything including num argument as well is in Global Execution Context so since now it’s in GEC, num can be accessed by Local memory for generatedFunc Ec to use it.
    - Nested Functions
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20266.png)
        
        - The point o notice hear is that when we try to find counter in local memory of incrementCounter’s EC its not there so its moves back to local memory of outer’s EC and finds counter there.
        
        Two things are possible here 
        
        - The incrementCounter is running inside of outer’s running so that we can access counter ion outer’s running
            
            OR
            
        - The incrementCounter is saved inside of EC of outer’s local memory.
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20267.png)
        
        - lets do some work on this example.
        - Just jump forward to point where myNewFucntion is called and inside its EC’s Thread of execution ( TEC ) we run counter++
        - Now is counter in EC of myNewFucntion’s local memory → NO
        - Is it in Global memory → NO
        
        Where is it then? 
        
        > When the function definition of incrementCounter is returned from outer it not only gets code for incrementCounter but also all of the environment around it as a backpack to the Global memory or where function outer was called.
        > 
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20268.png)
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20269.png)
        
        - When myNewFunction is called again the increment is done to counter present in backpack of the function Global memory.
        
        > This backpack is stored as `[[scope]]` → **a hidden property** attached to the function definition. Its should be kept remembered that it cannot be accessed like myNewFucntion.backpack.counter etc.
        > 
        - The only way we access it is by calling function which looks for it first in local memory and then moves up the scope until it founds variable in memory ( it is global memory in our case ).
- FAQs
    - If a variable is declared in outer but never referenced in incrementCounter
        
        It will never be added to backpack for incrementCounter or myNewFunction ( in Global memory ) because was never referenced in incrementCounter function’s definition.  
        
- Closure Technical Terms and Definition
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20270.png)
    
    - Closed over Variable Environment
        
        > The backpack with function definition is called as closed over variable environment.
        > 
    - Persistent
        
        > counter variable in C.O.V.E is Persistent Scope Referenced Data ( P.S.R.D )
        > 
    - Lexical or static scoping
        
        > The data a function has access to wherever it runs is determined by the fact  where it was physically defined in the code and which variables it had access to at that physical space.
        > 
    - Backpack is the result of JS being a lexically scoped language ( one that brings the data with function wherever that function goes)
    
    This whole thing of how the backpack was created is collectively called **`Closure`.** But in reality, only a backpack is what we should call Closure ( standard is not like this, unfortunately 😓 ). 
    
- Individual Backpacks
    
    Every function has its own individual backpack
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20271.png)
    
    - anotherFunction is returned incrementCounter function definition whose backpack was brand new as outer was called again ( forming new EC for itself and re declaring counter as 0 in memory )
- Applications
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20272.png)
    
    1. Can allow us to use some conditions to only run a function once ( like setting the counter to one and then checking in next call if it’s one, do not execute the function ).
    2. Memorization → If a cumbersome heavy calculation task is done once we can have it in our backpack allowing us to not run it again, saving memory, and time and being efficient.
    3. Iterators are just functions that return us 1st, second, 3rd, and so on elements of an array and how is that ? only because of backpack where it has a counter.
    4. Generators allows to pause a running function and come back to it when needed ( again using backpack )
    5. Module pattern allows to persist state for the life of an application.
    6. Asynchronous JavaScript

### Promises

The solution is Promises 

- How?
    - So the fetch does two things as mentioned in the picture
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20280.png)
        
    - It does initiate requests in the browser but also returns an object back in JS ( called as **Promise** ). This object is later filled with data we get from request ( Web Browser )
- Example
    
    As discussed before promise→ fetch ( Façade for Network requests ) does two things
    
    - Returns an object which has two properties
        - value
        - onFulfilled → empty array/.
            
            ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20281.png)
            
    - Make network requests using Web Browser feature using address which consists of
        - Domain ( [twitter.com](http://twitter.com) )
        - Path ( /will/tweets/1 )
        - Request method ( default → GET )
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20282.png)
        
- example then
    - previously the issue was how will we know if data hash come back
    - This is where that empty array onFulfilled, it can contain a function which gets triggered using JavaScript when data comes back.
    - Normally what we would do is use futureData.onFulfilled.push(OurSpecificCallback()), but in reality, it cannot be done as onFulfilled is a hidden property. But yeah bts it is what happens actually.
    
    > The method which help us does above is → then. Whatever is passed as input to it is stuck in that onFulfilled array. So futureData.then(display) goes directly to onFulfilled.
    > 
    > 
    > ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20283.png)
    > 
    
- Intuition of Asynchronous JavaScript
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20284.png)
    
    - Steps ( Vertical Height represents Time Passed → Green )
        
        Global Memory
        
        - display, printHello, blockFor300ms functions are declared.
        
        TEC ( 0ms )
        
        - setTimeout is called which sets the timer in Web Browser Features and attaches the printHello function with Timer.
        
        Web Browser Features
        
        - Timer is set to 0ms.
        - Therefore it’s completed, onCompletion printHello function is moved to **Callback Queue**.
        
        TEC ( 1ms )
        
        - futureData is assigned what we get back from fetch (  a facade for Web Browser Feature → Network Request )
        - JavaScript
            - is a Promise object containing value and onFulfilled  ( empty array ) fields.
        - Web Browser Features ( 1ms )
            - Sends a request to the address provided to fetch i.e. domain and path at
            - Is it completed? No.
        - futureData.then is passed display which goes to the onFulfilled array in promise object.
        
        Global Memory
        
        - The promise object is assigned to futureData.
        
        TEC ( 2ms )
        
        - BlockFor300ms function is called and gets executed for 300ms.
        
        Web Browser Features ( 270ms )
        
        - data gets back from Twitter, completed, and futureData.value gets the “hi” string.
        - Then passed to display in onFulfilled as a argument and pushed to microtask queue
        
        TEC (302ms) 
        
        - console.log(”Me first”).
        - **Since all synchronous code is done now will pick display from the microtask queue** and run with the argument “hi” string.
        - then printHello from the callback queue.
        
        > Any Function that is attached to promise object by one of the two pronged facade function wither js or Web browser features ( like display was put in promise object using .then ) all go to microtask queue.
        > 
        
        > Any function that is passed directly to the facade function that triggers a Web Browser feature like a callback to TimeOut function goes to the callback queue.
        > 
        
         
        
- OnRejection is another empty array where function passed to futureData.catch() go moved to microtask queue to run in case there is some kind of error **OR** or ****passed as second argument to the .then function. ****

- Prototype Chain
    
    Solution 2:
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20294.png)
    
    1. Store the function increment in another object. When user1 calls method increment and does not find it in its object it automatically goes to functionStore object and finds increment there ? but how does it finds it.
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20295.png)
        
    2. Using the Object.create() we pass functionStore to it so that increment function is not there by default in every user but once we need it, it is founc in the functionStore object and somehow each user is gonna link to share functionStore object.
    3. When object.create(functionStore) is called its just an empty object but bts its linked to functionStore in someway.
    4. Actually there is a hidden property named ***__proto__*** which has stored a link to functionStore object.
    
    > Prototype Chain means that when js do not finds a property in an object its chekcs reference in the __proto__ property of the object to get to the object which contains that property.
    > 
    
    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20296.png)
    
    - Implicit Parameters in Prototype Chain
        - When we are calling increment for let say user 456 or 123 how its gonna know which user score has to be incremented because we are not passing user object as input to this function right ?
        - There comes an **Implicit Parameter.** which is not provided by us but its automatically there.
        
        > This is assigned as value as whatever the object is on left hand side.
        > 
        > 
        > ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20297.png)
        > 
        
         
        
    - hasOwnProperty method
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20298.png)
        
        - there is no property either we set or we saw in the object for users such as hasOwnProperty so where does it come from?
        
        > Every object in JavaScript has a __proto__ property which has default link to Object.prototype object having some useful functions.
        > 
        - In our case user1 has not this property so its visits __proto__ reference to user function store and then object.prototype object to get hasOwnProperty() method ( which has proto but null as no further reference needed ) due to JavaScript’s prototypic nature
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20299.png)
        
    - this keyowrd
        
        ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20300.png)
        
        - Just put this.score in a sub function so ( to make a point) that we can use functions inside increment method as well.
        - Bu this keyowrd inside add is assigned window ( Global memory ) where window.score is undefined as its not in global memory at all ? normally in other languages it would not happen but in JS it does 😄
        - Th eold sol was to use That and assign this of that local memory ( increment’s ) adn using that.score which was not found in add and looks up in the increment to find it and use it instead.
        - Modern way to use add1.call() and pass this as argument ( this → user1 ) so it evaluated to user1. and now this from the add1 local memory is assigned user1.
        
        > If there is a an object to left side of a method call like in user1.increment, this keyword is assigned that object otherwise its assigned global object ( window ) except when function was defined as arrow function.
        > 
    - Arrow Function Scope and this
        - For case of arrow function, its this is lexically scope means
        
        > what *this* of the arrow function is assigned to depends on where arrow function is defined, in our case if its saved or defined in increment, there *this* is assigned user1 so here we end up using user1 ( this ) directly.
        > 
        > 
        > ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20301.png)
        > 
        - Rule of thumb
            
            > method of objects are and should not defined as arrow functions as they will end up assigning their this with global object which is not what we want, we want their this to be assigned with object calling them.
            >

        - Mental Model Shift
            - 1 is multiplied by 2 and then combined with an empty array. How do we combine a number and an array ? by pushing number into array.
                
                ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20313.png)
                
            - After that we simply multiple 2 by 2 and then push into combined array and result 1 * 2 and so on. So its same array being pushed with elements after an operation on them.
            - Now how it relates the reduce function, let us understand it.
                
                ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20314.png)
                
                - At first iteration we have an empty array ( accumulator ) and result of an element applied some operation on . So here we are reducing two things array and element = one array with an element. This is what reduce does.
                - The accumulator (  the thing which we are combining with ) or the one which is common to reduction as input ( like array in our case is same in each reduction process while numbers are different every time ).
                - `Reduction` is not obtaining whole resultant array of [ 2, 4, 6] but its only each individual process of combining two things ( array and number ) to get an array with a number in it. While repeating it continuously gets us our whole resultant array.
                - `Reducer` is the rule by which we combine two things to become one.
                    
                    ![Untitled](Learning/JavaScript/attachments/Untitled%20315.png)

    - Closure Clarification
        - Function, objects and arrays etc are stored in heap.
        
        > Heap: a much larger part of the memory that stores everything allocated dynamically, that allows a faster code execution, and protects it from corruption and makes the execution faster.
        > 
        - we saying that add3 was passed back to global memory is not true it only means that a reference of where its stored ( heap ) is passed to global memory and we can use that reference to access it.
        
    - Inner Function
        
        
    
    > There is always a back pack attached to a function.
    > 
    - And this is what the concept of Closure is where the kind of data a function has access to directly relates to where it was defined.
    - Lile incrementCounter was defined inside outer so it aurely has access to counter when its returned from outer into global, through a backpack.
    
    ### Data
    
    - There are two kinds of data a function has access to
    - Temporary in form of Execution context which goes away as soon as its done being executed.
    - the other is persistent storage which is what we for now call as backpack.
    - 
    - The backpack is accessed through a property named `scope` which is private and hidden as well.
    - But bts it is what has a link to these backpack variables.
    
    ### Garbage
    
    Data which has no label avaialble so that it can be accessed is garbage. 
    
    - Only variables which are used by function from its surrounding environment will be
    - Exercise
        
        [CS Bin](http://csbin.io/functional)
        
         
        
         
        
    
    > This data which `scope` refers is the data which was available to function when it was initially stored in memory i.e. The data around it and it is what we call lexical or static scope. Its `fixed` from when function was saved ( do not changes over time ). Its lexical because where ever we save our function ( the physical place ) determines which data it has access to. Thus called `Static Lexical Scope`. Keeping in mind that its also persistent thus collectively called `P.L.S.R.D`: `Persistent Lexical Scope Referenced Data`. Tis backpack is also called as `Closed Over Variable Environment` or `C.O.V.E`. Standard is `Closure`.
    > 
    
    > Lexical Scope is feature that enables the  existence of `backpack` or `PLSRD` or `COVE`.
    >

## How understanding JS is important for us

lets take an example how does it works 

Consider:

x = "5";
y = x++;

That inaccurate mental model would have predicted `x` as "51" ("5" + 1) and `y` as just "5".

Instead x will end up as `6`, and `y` will be `5`, not "5".

The spec says `y = x++` is basically:

y = Number(x);
x = Number(x) + 1;

### typeof

![Untitled](Untitled%20395.png)

`returns type of the value in v`

- `undefined` means v currently has no value ( it may have but is now made undefined or its just declared )
- All return values from `typeof` are themselves `string`. ( effectively it returns only a very small portion of string type ) so it can never return `undefined` or `null` as it always returns it in string type `"undefined".`
- `typeof` returns `null` as `object` ?? which is weird but in specs its mentioned that
    
    > When setting  regular value like number you would use `undefined` while for objects unset them using `null`.
    > 

![Untitled](Untitled%20396.png)

![Untitled](Untitled%20397.png)

### Undefined vs Undeclared vs Uninitialized ( TDZ )

- `Undefined` means that something exists but is not initialized a value.
- `Undeclared` means something never existed.
- But in JS both cases are denoted by `undefined` → total absurdity.
- Certain variables do not get initialized at all ( blocked scope like `let` and `const` ). They never get set to `undefined` ( this place where they are `uninitialized` or can never be accessed is called `Temporal Dead Zone`).

### Special Types ( NAN )

- `NAN -> Not a number` essentially indicates that given value is an invalid number.
    
    ![Untitled](Untitled%20398.png)
    
- `NAN` does not hold `identity` property thus is not equal to itself, At least only is JS
- `isNAN` helps us identify a `nan`.
- But it has an issue that it coerces the value as Number first ( which in case of string it definitely coerces it to NAN ) and then checks if isNAN or not thus even string is a `true` which should not happen.
- So ES6 introduced a better version of it which uses `Number.isNAN`
- `typeof` of NAN is `number` ? yeah its a number but invalid one, If its not a valid number this does not mean that its not even a number.

> Whenever designing a system where you have no specific value to return as a number return `NAN` .The absence of valid number is only `NAN`
> 

![Untitled](Untitled%20399.png)

### Negative Zero

- just like the `nan` also part of IEEE  754.
- Was ignored by early JS versions.
    
    ![Untitled](Untitled%20400.png)
    
- All the conditions above except line 2 do not make sense ( how can `-0 === 0 true` )
- `-0 < 0 → true` but not in js
- The only way to really or truly check `-0` is using `Object.is()` in ES6.
- Where the hell wo ever use this ?
    
    Let see an example for instance you have to represent the direction of a car when it has stopped. The only way to represent opposite direction is `-0`
    
- `Math.sign()` is used to find if a number has a negative bit.
    
    ![Untitled](Untitled%20401.png)
    
    ![Untitled](Untitled%20402.png)
    

### Exercise

```jsx
# Polyfill for `Object.is(..)`

In this exercise, you will define a polyfill for `Object.is(..)`. No cheating and looking it up online!

## Instructions

1. `Object.is(..)` should take two parameters.

2. It should return `true` if the passed in parameters are exactly the same value (not just `===` -- see below!), or `false` otherwise.

3. For `NaN` testing, you can use `Number.isNaN(..)`, but first see if you can find a way to test without usage of any utility?

4. For `-0` testing, no built-in utility exists, but here's a hint: `-Infinity`.

5. If the parameters are any other values, just test them for strict equality.

6. You cannot use the built-in `Object.is(..)` -- that's cheating!

## Polyfill Pattern

**NOTE:** Since your JS environment probably already has `Object.is(..)`, to test your polyfill you'll have to first unconditionally define it (no `if` guard), and then add the `if` guard when you're done.

To define a polyfill, it looks like this:

```js
if (!Object.is) {
	Object.is = function ObjectIs(..) { .. };
}
```
```

Although i coulndn’t do it here is how its solved

```jsx
if (!Object.is /*|| true*/) {
	Object.is = function ObjectIs(x,y) {
		var xNegZero = isItNegZero(x);
		var yNegZero = isItNegZero(y);

		if (xNegZero || yNegZero) {
			return xNegZero && yNegZero;
		}
		else if (isItNaN(x) && isItNaN(y)) {
			return true;
		}
		else if (x === y) {
			return true;
		}

		return false;

		// **********

		function isItNegZero(x) {
			return x === 0 && (1 / x) === -Infinity;
		}

		function isItNaN(x) {
			return x !== x;
		}
	};
}

    - The expression `1 < 2 < 3` gives true ? it is right but similar if returned around does not work for `3 > 2 > 1` why ?
        - What happens bts is that `1 < 2` ⇒ evaluated to `true` while since next operand is a number thus `true` is `coerced` to number `1` which by chance is less than `3` thus total result is by chance `true`
        - now `3 > 2` true but that coerced to `1 > 1` is not true but `false`
        - so implicit boolean coercion to `numbers` is a terrible mistake.

### Philosophy of Cercerion

![Untitled](Untitled%20436.png)

- Writing quality JS code means to always take care of coercion, functions should be ones where each function deals with one type only like numbers or strings etc.
- JS dynamic type system is not a weakness but its strength.
- Code comments should be there, but code itself should not be that complex that it must need a comment to explain itself.
- Comments should be telling the why part and not the what part
- Implicit coercion is not bad but is considered to be worse and compared with explicit type castings of Java and C++
- So in simple words abstractions are nothing but behind the scene of Implicit Coercions.

### Solution Mine

```jsx
function isValidName(name){
    if(name === undefined || name === null || name === "" || typeof name !== "string"){
        return false;
    }else
    {
        if(name.trim().length >= 3){
            return true;
        }else{
            return false;
        }
    }
}
function hoursAttended(attended, length){
    if((typeof attended === 'string' || typeof attended === 'number') || (typeof length === 'string' || typeof length === 'number') ){
        if(attended === undefined || length === undefined || attended === null || length === null || attended === "" || length === "" ){
            return false;
        }else{
            attended = Number(attended);
            length = Number(length);

            if(isNaN(attended) || isNaN(length)){
                return false;
            }else
            {
                if(attended < 0 || length < 0){
                    return false;
                }
                else if(attended > length){
                    return false;
                }else if(Number.isInteger(attended) && Number.isInteger(length)){
                    if(attended <= length){
                        return true;
                    }
                }else{
                    return false;
                }

            }
            

        }
    }else{
        return false;
    }
}
```

### Solution Kyle Simson

```jsx
function isValidName(name) {
	if (
		typeof name == "string" &&
		name.trim().length >= 3
	) {
		return true;
	}

	return false;
}

function hoursAttended(attended,length) {
	if (
		typeof attended == "string" &&
		attended.trim() != ""
	) {
		attended = Number(attended);
	}
	if (
		typeof length == "string" &&
		length.trim() != ""
	) {
		length = Number(length);
	}
	if (
		typeof attended == "number" &&
		typeof length == "number" &&
		attended <= length &&
		attended >= 0 &&
		length >= 0 &&
		Number.isInteger(attended) &&
		Number.isInteger(length)
	) {
		return true;
	}

	return false;
}
```

### Advanced Scope

### Lexical Scope

### Intuition

> Something that is fixed at author time ( compile time ) and its predictable and do not gets affected by the runtime conditions.
> 

### Dynamic Scope ( Opposite of Lexical Scope )

> Runtime conditions are going to affect the scope in fact.
> 

### Lexical Scope

![Untitled](Untitled%20495.png)

The value teacher used in the ask function is decided at the compile time and this is actually how `Lexical Scope` works in fact. 

### Dynamic Scope

![Untitled](Untitled%20496.png)

Considering if dynamic scope did existed in js then

- `teacher` in `ask` function would resolve to use `Suzy` value instead of `Kyle`.
- a function’s references to its variables are depending upon where that function was called from. That is why wherever ask is called will decide what value `teacher` will have.
- 

### Explanation of difference in both

the key difference lies in how the enclosing scope is determined.

Let's revisit the example to clarify the difference:

```jsx

x = 10

function foo():
    print(x)

function bar():
    x = 20
    foo()

bar()  # Prints different values based on scope rules
```

In lexical (static) scope:

- When **`foo`** is called from **`bar`**, it looks for the variable **`x`** in its own scope (**`foo`**). Since it doesn't find **`x`** in its scope, it moves up to the next enclosing scope, which is the global scope. It finds **`x`** with the value **`10`** in the global scope and prints that value.

In dynamic scope:

- When **`foo`** is called from **`bar`**, it looks for the variable **`x`** in its own scope (**`foo`**). Since it doesn't find **`x`** in its scope, it looks up the call stack to find the calling function, which is **`bar`**. It finds **`x`** with the value **`20`** in the scope of **`bar`** and prints that value.

So, the key difference here is that in lexical scope, the scope of a variable is determined by its location in the source code (where it's defined), while in dynamic scope, the scope of a variable is determined by the order of function calls in the runtime call stack.

### Principle of Least Exposure

The Principle of Least Exposure, also known as the Principle of Least Privilege or the Principle of Minimal Privilege, is a concept in computer security and software design that suggests limiting the access and permissions granted to entities (such as users, processes, or programs) to the bare minimum necessary for them to perform their tasks effectively and no more.

In essence, this principle promotes the idea that entities should only have access to the resources and data that are directly required for their functionality and nothing beyond that. By adhering to the Principle of Least Exposure, you can reduce the potential risks and negative impacts of security breaches, unauthorized access, and unintended consequences.

Key points of the Principle of Least Exposure include:

1. **Minimizing Access:** Users or programs should only be given the least amount of access rights required to accomplish their tasks. This reduces the attack surface and potential damage if a breach occurs.
2. **Need-to-Know Basis:** Users should only be granted access to data and resources that are relevant to their role and responsibilities. This helps prevent data leakage and exposure.
3. **Default Deny:** Systems should be configured to deny access by default and grant access only to specific approved entities. This approach enhances security by ensuring that only authorized actions are allowed.
4. **Separation of Privileges:** Separating different privileges or roles helps prevent a single compromised component from gaining access to all system resources.
5. **Regular Review:** Access rights and permissions should be reviewed periodically to ensure that they remain aligned with current needs and to remove unnecessary privileges.
6. **Least Common Mechanism:** Avoid sharing resources or mechanisms between entities whenever possible, as this can minimize the potential impact of a compromise.

The Principle of Least Exposure applies not only to security practices but also to software design and development. When designing software systems, you should limit the visibility and accessibility of components, functions, and variables to only those parts of the system that truly need them. This can improve modularity, maintainability, and overall system stability.

By adhering to the Principle of Least Exposure, you can create more secure and robust systems while reducing the potential for security breaches and unauthorized access.

### How Principle of Least Exposure helps us

Third point of it is → if you hide its implementation details then you save  yourself from future restriction of refactoring of it in future , Because if you do someone’s code is definitely gonna break.  Thus hiding it allows you to freely refactor it later on.

### Preference of Hoisting Techniques

- We are using both variable hoisting and function hoisting here i.e. using vars and functions before their actual declarations.
- Variable hoisting is common but people tend to avoid function hoisting, well you should not, its recommended and a better thing to call show executable code before its declaration to make it easier for user to understand or use it.

![Untitled](Untitled%20511.png)

### Let doesn’t hoist ?

- Well for it to not hoist means code below at line 4 should print `Kyle` as since `teacher` inside block isn’t hoisted ( noted down during compilation step ) then
- Line 4 should move to outer scope to look for `teacher` but it doesn’t do that and just throws TDZ error.
- Two differences why it happens
    - Let and cosnt hoist to blocks while var to function.
    - During compilation step var assigns undefined to `identifier` unless it sees the declaration while `let, const` assign nothing and leave `identifier` as un-initialized unless it sees declaration → which leads to `TDZ ( Temporal Dead Zone )`

![Untitled](Untitled%20512.png)

### Why TZD error

- TDZ exists because of `const` and not `let`
- Becuase if const is initialized to `undefined` , according to its core definition i.e. not to be able to assign ever again will be violated when you will assign a value later on upon seeing a declaration.
- So always put `let` and `const` at top of the line.

### Why function expression can be hoisted

- Because we cannot predict something which has to happen when we reach there only, expression is an executable, so it conceptually be re-ordered it will run when you will have it ( reach it ).
- Hoisting only reference declarative things and not executable code becuase executables have to happen always at run-time.
- Something that has to happen at line 13 can’t happen at line 2 as i will distort the whole program order
- It does not mean that compile time does not handle the function expression, it is handled ( created a scope and have a plan of things happening)
- What didn’t happen is that it does not get associated with an identifier at compile time as it cannot be possible ( explained previously ).
- All functions have a plan (a map or plan become a thing in memory when executed)for their execution before they get executed.

- Definition

    - The second component is inner function ask which is closed over some variables like teacher and question. We can access ask using the workshop but we cannot access teacher and question variables.
    - In short using public api object we are exposing only a subset of things like in our case only ask while all other entities are private.

### Implicit and Explicit Binding

- **Namespace pattern ( Flexible )**

![Untitled](Untitled%20527.png)

- The usage of object to call a function allows to point `this` keyword to point at the object which called the function.
    - workshop.ask → says invoke `ask` with the `this` keyword pointing at `workshop`
    - This is what Implicit Binding, allows to share behavior in different contexts.
    
    ![Untitled](Untitled%20528.png)
    
- **Explicit Binding of `this` keyword**
    - Here its predictable that which things are assigned to `this` keyword. Now we are specifying context. Now it does not matter from where the function is coming
        
        ![Untitled](Untitled%20529.png)
        
- Hard Biding ( variation of explicit binding )
    - Actually the line 8 not actual call site for which is definitely not gonna be workshop.ask so ask will not be invoked in workshop context.
    - So we get undefined. Technically `setTimeout`  is defined by Html to not invoke it with default call but `.call` with Global EC like window but it actually explicitly invokes it with a .call in the context of gloabal. So workshop.ask is invoke [cb.call](http://cb.call) window.
    
    ![Untitled](Untitled%20530.png)
    
    - Line 11 uses hard bind function, actually `bind` does not invoke this function but produces new function which is bound to particular this context specified.
    - But it takes away flexibility so that `this` always will be assigned to `workshop` object no matter the place it is called from and now its completely predictable.

For Dynamicism use `this` and for predictability we can use lexical scope or closure.

## Prototypes

### Intuition

![Untitled](Untitled%20543.png)

- As we know using new in front of function creates an object for binding with `this` of that function call.
- Lets go back to Class theory
    - Class is a abstract pattern for a thing, like a blueprint.
    - Instance is taking this blueprint to build something → concrete thing not abstract.
    - class-oriented operation is fundamentally a copy operation.
    - Lets take an example to understand it
        
        > When a building is built using the blueprint, once its built then if we make any change in either the blueprint or the building would any one affect the other → obviously not. This implies → their relation just ended once we instantiated the class ( copied all the behaviors of class )
        > 
- In JS there is no copying at all when an object is instantiated. So when a constructor call makes an object it does not makes it ~~based on~~ but linked to the `proptotype` .
- So actually linking and copying is entirely different thing.

## Question for this & Prototype

### Scope of Variable in a Arrow function

- Arrow functions do have lexical scope
- They do not posses a `this` keyword.
- Arrow functions do not have prototype unlike all other function may they be anonymous or named.
    - This is why using `new` keyword does work. Because it is not a constructor that can be constructed or it does not have a prototype.

### In `this` aware callback, does value of `this` depends on how higher order function calls the callback

- Call site matters
- Like passing a function in say `.map` , how `.map` invokes your callback determines the `this` binding. Unless we have passed a hard bound function using `.bind`
- Higher order functions like .map, .filter, .reduce does determine what will be the context of `this` keyword.

### What happens when we set dunder proto / __proto__

- Not advised to use it as a setter, though it is both a setter and getter.
- Its an anti-pattern to re-wire the prototype chain of an object.
- But in ES6 we can use it to set the proto linkage from one object to other.
- We can use `Oject.setPrototypeOf()`

### Inheritance is Delegation

- JavaScript classes are actually Prototypal System which is in fact a Delegation System and not a class system.
- Prototypal or Delegation system is way more powerful than a class system when it comes to comparison. Its like Prototypal System is a `Super set` and Class is a `Subset` becuase we did make class system using Prototypal System but reverse is not possible.

## Delegation Pattern

- Imagine a login page where we want to have auth controller and login form controller which dentoes all ui stuff
- The old school way would be since we need both of these together so will make one parent and other child class. Where child class will be instantiated to have object containing all method and properties of both.

![Untitled](Untitled%20560.png)

- The new way would be to have composition over inheritance instead of composition through inheritance.
- So diffrent classes for each and then instantiate both and make one instance as property of other one. In this way we again have access to all methods and properties of both in one place

### Mixin Composition

### Delegation Pattern

- According to it we think as peer-to-peer instead of Parent-child.

![Untitled](Untitled%20562.png)

- So both are objects where LoginFormController is linked to AuthController thorugh Prototype Chain.
- Why are we doing this is to make sure they can cooperate with each other, use properties of one another without any issue.

### The DOM

![Untitled](Untitled%20568.png)

- Simply a memory representation of your HTML.

> Dom is a structure in memory that browser create when they are rendering a page.
> 

  

![Untitled](Untitled%20569.png)

> API, a list of functions and properties available under different objects that browser exposes to us which we can manipulate.
> 
- We can change the structure in memory, add or remove elements in memory.
- This will trigger an update in the rendering HTML that you see on the screen. Its actually quick and dirty but its like changing your HTML.
- On the contrast in reality we are changing a memory representation, but it looks like we are changing HTML.

The DOM API is available on many objects.

- We have global object named `Window Global Object` .
- The `window` keyword represents browser `window` from late 90s because tab concept was not there at that time. So for one page there was one browser window and for two pages we have another browser window.
- So we can call it navigation system approximately not accurately.
- `document` object is DOM, so a structure. In 90s we used to have only one document per window, but these days we can have more than one document in same page navigation. This `document` object represents current `DOM`

DOM api is available on every object in the DOM. Each HtmL element has one object.

![Untitled](Untitled%20570.png)

- For third point `Triggering updates in user interface when thread is released`
    - In case of Virtual Dom ( clone of real DOM ) managed completely by JavaScript, Its like an array or collection in memory. No direct relationship with Real DOM.
    - Its beleived that if we make multiple changes at once in Virtual DOM, react will updates Real Dom only once which is more performant that Vanilla JS.
    - While in reality if we are changing the same property multiple times in same execution context, the real dom will just take the last one. Showing us only the last change.
    - though this is not same as Virtual Dom in terms of performance.
